**How to Quantify Mitochondrial Numbers Per Cell** Below you’ll find a practical “tool‑kit” covering three complementary approaches: | Method | What it measures | Typical workflow | Strengths | Limitations | |--------|------------------|-------------------|-----------|-------------| | **Fluorescence microscopy + automated segmentation** | Number of fluorescent puncta per nucleus | Stain live/dead cells → capture z‑stacks → segment nuclei & mitochondria → count | Fast; works on many cell types; high throughput | Requires good signal/noise; overlapping organelles may merge | | **Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM)** | Direct visual counts of individual mitochondria | Fixation → resin embedding → ultrathin section → TEM imaging → manual / semi‑automatic counting | Gold standard – resolves cristae, morphology | Laborious; low field of view; expensive | | **mtDNA:nuclear DNA ratio via quantitative PCR (qPCR)** | Relative copy number of mtDNA vs nDNA | Isolate total DNA → duplex qPCR targeting MT–ND1 (or COX I) & single‑copy nuclear gene (β‑actin, GAPDH) → ΔCt calculation | High sensitivity; no need for imaging | Assumes constant ploidy; cannot distinguish intact vs fragmented mitochondria | --- ### 1️⃣ Fluorescent Imaging Workflow #### A. Reagents & Equipment | Item | Notes | |------|-------| | **MitoTracker™ Red CMXRos** (Thermo Fisher) or **Mitotracker Green FM** | Concentration 100 nM (optimize). Works best at 37 °C. | | **Hoechst 33342** or **DAPI** | Nuclear counterstain. | | **Live‑Cell Imaging System** (confocal or spinning disk) | Acquire Z‑stack (~0.5 µm spacing). | | **ImageJ/Fiji** + **TrackMate**, **CellProfiler** | For segmentation/counting. | | Optional: **Flow Cytometer** (for bulk measurement) | If you prefer population statistics over images. | #### B. Protocol ```text 1. Plate ~10⁴–2×10⁵ cells/well on glass-bottom dishes (35 mm). 2. Incubate overnight at 37 °C, 5% CO₂. 3. Prepare staining solution: - Dilute Mitotracker (100 nM) in pre-warmed phenol-free DMEM. - Add Hoechst/DAPI (50 ng/mL) simultaneously. 4. Replace culture media with dye-containing buffer; incubate 30 min at 37 °C. 5. Wash twice with warm PBS to remove excess dye. 6. Image immediately (avoid photobleaching): - Excitation/emission: Mitotracker R (561 nm/590 nm), DAPI (405 nm/461 nm). 7. Capture ≥20 random fields per condition (≥200 cells total). ``` #### C. Data Analysis Pipeline (Fiji) 1. **Open stack** → `Process > Duplicate` → duplicate into two stacks (mito & nucleus). 2. **Background subtraction** (`Subtract Background`) → set rolling ball radius ≈ 50 px. 3. **Threshold** each stack separately (`Auto Threshold`, Otsu). 4. **Convert to binary** → `Binary > Make Binary`. 5. **Morphological operations** (`Erode`, `Dilate`) to separate touching objects. 6. **Analyze Particles** (`Analyze > Analyze Particles…`) * Size filter: 0.02–5 µm² (adjust per resolution) * Circularity: 0.3–1.00 * Output: Count, area, mean intensity. 7. Export results → Excel/Pandas → compute average mito/nucleus ratio. > **Tip:** Automating this pipeline in CellProfiler allows batch processing across dozens of plates. #### D. Troubleshooting * **Low Signal:** Increase dye concentration up to 250 nM but watch toxicity (>500 nM kills cells). * **High Background:** Ensure thorough washing; use fresh dye solutions. * **Overlapping Organelles:** Switch to super-resolution confocal or Airyscan; alternatively, deconvolve raw images before thresholding. --- ### 2️⃣ Transmission EM Counting #### A. Sample Prep Highlights 1. **Fixation**: 2.5% glutaraldehyde in 0.1 M cacodylate buffer, pH 7.4, 1 h at RT. 2. **Post-fix**: 1% osmium tetroxide, 45 min. 3. **Dehydration**: graded ethanol series → propylene oxide. 4. **Embedding**: Epon resin; polymerize 48 h @60 °C. 5. **Sectioning**: Ultramicrotome → 70 nm sections onto copper grids. 6. **Staining**: Uranyl acetate (25 mg/ml, 30 min) → lead citrate (5 min). #### B. Imaging & Counting * Use a JEOL/JSM microscope at 80 kV. * Randomly select 10–12 non-overlap areas per grid (≈400 px × 400 px). * Manually trace mitochondria boundaries or use Fiji’s `Segmentation Editor`. * Record counts per area → convert to per-cell basis assuming known cell density from parallel light‑microscopy measurements. > **Note:** Because only thin slices are imaged, apply stereology correction factors (Cavalieri principle) if absolute counts are required. --- ### 3️⃣ mtDNA Copy Number by qPCR #### A. Primer Design | Target | Sequence (forward/reverse) | Amplicon size | |--------|----------------------------|---------------| | **MT‑ND1** | F: AGGAGATGGAAACCTTCCCA
R: TTTGTTCACCATTGCCTCAT | 120 bp | | **B2M** (single-copy nuclear) | F: GCGACTTGGAAGAAGGTAAC
R: TGCAAAGGTACTGCCAAGAA | 110 bp | Validate primers (ΔTm ≤ 1 °C, efficiency 90–105%). #### B. DNA Extraction Use Qiagen QIAamp DNA Mini Kit or equivalent. Include RNase treatment to avoid RNA contamination. #### C. Duplex qPCR Setup ```text Reaction mix (per well, 20 μl): - SYBR® Master Mix (Applied Biosystems): 10 μl - Forward primer (10 mM): 0.8 μl (final 400 nM) - Reverse primer (10 mM): 0.8 μl - Template DNA: 2 ng - Nuclease-free water: adjust volume Cycling conditions: 95 °C 10 s 58 °C 30 s 72 °C 30 s Repeat x40 cycles Melting curve 65–95 °C ``` Run standards (serial dilutions of plasmid containing both targets) to generate calibration curves. #### D. Calculations Let Ct_mt = cycle threshold for MT‑ND1, Ct_nuc = Ct for B2M. \[ \Delta \mathrm{Ct}= \mathrm{Ct}_{\text{mt}}-\mathrm{Ct}_{\text{nuc}} \] Assuming equal amplification efficiencies, \[ \frac{\text{mtDNA copies}}{\text{nDNA copies}}=2^{-\Delta \mathrm{Ct}} \] If one wants an estimate of mitochondria per cell, multiply by the average mtDNA copies per mitochondrion (typically 2–10 depending on species/cell type). This gives a rough *relative* value rather than an exact integer. --- ### 4️⃣ Choosing the Right Approach | Scenario | Recommended method(s) | |----------|---------------------| | Rapid screening of multiple lines | Fluorescence microscopy + automated counting | | Detailed morphological assessment | TEM | | Large-scale comparative studies where imaging isn’t feasible | qPCR mtDNA:nDNA ratio | | Single-cell precision | Flow cytometric detection of MitoTracker+ events combined with gating on forward scatter (size) | --- ### 5️⃣ Practical Tips & Common Pitfalls | Issue | Solution | |-------|---------| | **Phototoxicity during live imaging** | Keep laser power minimal (<1 %) and limit exposure time. | | **Uneven plating leading to variable cell densities** | Seed uniformly; verify confluency under phase contrast before staining. | | **Counting bias due to overlapping mitochondria** | Deconvolution or higher NA objectives help resolve clusters. | | **Variability in mtDNA content between subpopulations** | Perform replicate experiments; normalize to housekeeping genes. | | **Data interpretation** | Always report median ± interquartile range; consider biological replicates (N≥3). | --- ### 6️⃣ Quick Reference Code Snippet (Python + scikit-image) ```python import numpy as np from skimage import io, filters, measure, morphology import pandas as pd def count_mito(img_path, nuc_img_path=None): img = io.imread(img_path) # Preprocess blur = filters.gaussian(img, sigma=1) thresh = filters.threshold_otsu(blur) bw = blur > thresh # Remove small artifacts cleaned = morphology.remove_small_objects(bw, min_size=20) labeled = measure.label(cleaned) props = measure.regionprops(labeled) counts = len(props) return counts # Example usage mit_counts = [count_mito(f'img_{i}.png') for i in range(1,21)] df = pd.DataFrame({'Field':range(1,21),'MitoCount':mit_counts}) print(df.describe()) ``` This script demonstrates how to automate counting for a batch of brightfield/fluorescence images—ideal when paired with your own custom thresholds. --- ### Final Thought Quantifying mitochondria accurately requires balancing **resolution**, **throughput**, and **resource availability**. Start with fluorescence-based counting for quick screens; validate key findings with TEM or qPCR. By integrating all three datasets, you gain confidence that observed changes reflect true alterations in mitochondrial abundance rather than technical artefacts. Happy experimenting!
